headline: Double Creek Fluke Keep Coming on the Drift — Kingfish and Blowfish Own Tices Shoal
subhead: Weakfish have slid off the sedges for the summer, but fluke, blowfish, and kingfish are keeping the rods bent from Oyster Creek to the inlet.
body_markdown:
I remember a July morning back when I was mating on the Point Pleasant boats, maybe sixteen years old, and the old skipper — Sal, everybody called him Sal the Greek even though he wasn't — told me the bay in high summer is a different animal than the bay in May. May, he said, the fish are moving through, hunting, hungry, and you can find them by accident. July, the bay settles into its bones. The water gets heavy and warm on top, the bait tucks into the grass, and if you don't know where the deep water runs cool you're just casting at ghosts. Forty years later I still hear him every time I idle past Tices Shoal in the middle of August and see the flat go glassy calm. That lesson never gets old, and it's exactly what's playing out on Barnegat Bay right now.

The fluke have been the most dependable thing going. Double Creek Channel is still the address — that stretch where the channel dog-legs south of the Route 37 bridge holds bait and current both, and on the last two hours of the ebb into the first hour of a new flood, the drift sets up clean. I've been running 3/4-ounce bucktails, chartreuse and white, tipped with a 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet in nuclear chicken, dragged slow along bottom in 10 to 14 feet. Keepers have been mixed in with a lot of shorts, so it's not a five-minute limit, but a patient drift will put two or three fluke in the 18 to 20-inch range in the cooler for an afternoon's work. The mouth of Oyster Creek has also been kicking out fluke on the last of the outgoing, when that warmer creek water pushes out over the flat and concentrates bait right where the channel drops off — spearing and small killies on a simple fishfinder rig work there if you don't want to bother with plastics.

Blowfish are doing what blowfish do in July, which is show up everywhere there's current and clam or squid on the bottom. Tices Shoal has been thick with them on the high incoming tide — anchor up along the edge of the shoal in six to eight feet, small hooks, squid strips cut thin, and you can fill a bucket in an evening if you've got the patience for the bite-and-miss game they play. Kids on the dock at Oyster Creek have been doing the same with strips of clam and having a ball with it. Kingfish have been mixing in on the ocean side — the beaches at Island Beach State Park and the inlet jetty rocks at Barnegat Light have both given up kingfish on bloodworms and Fishbites, high-low rigs, right in that skinny wash where the sand drops off. The ocean's been running around 73 degrees off the Jersey coast the last check I had, which is right in the kingfish's comfort zone, and that water's pushing plenty of sand fleas and worms up onto the beach for them to work.

Bluefish have shown up in fits — bunker schools have been rolling through Barnegat Inlet on the tide changes, and where you find the bunker balled up tight near the surface, you'll find blues underneath cutting them to pieces. Ava jigs, the 007 size, worked with a jigging stroke right through the school, will draw strikes, and if you want cocktail blues for the kids, small Kastmasters off the bulkheads near the inlet at first light have been steady. Nothing gigantic — mostly 2 to 4 pounds — but they hit hard and they're around most mornings this week.

Now the honest part. Weakfish, which were thick around the sedge banks back in May the way they always are, have thinned way out. That's normal — they don't hang around the bay all summer the way some folks expect. A few stragglers are still showing after dark on bucktails tipped with squid strips worked slow along the edges of Double Creek and the deeper holes off Good Luck Point, but I wouldn't plan a whole trip around weakfish right now. If you want them, fish the last hour of light into full dark and keep your expectations modest.

Stripers are the toughest call of the week. Summer heat in the bay pushes them out — they don't love water in the high 70s any more than we'd love a July day in a wool coat. The better play has been the inlet itself, working the jetty rocks and the deeper water off Barnegat Light before sunrise, live bunker on a fish-finder rig or bucktails worked deep along the rock edges where the current runs hardest. It's not a sure thing and it's not a numbers game, but the fish that do show are usually solid, mid-20s to low 30s, holding tight to structure where the current breaks.

Looking ahead, if the wind stays out of the southwest and lays down like it has the last few days, I'd keep working Double Creek on the tide changes for fluke — that pattern's been the most consistent thing on the bay all month. Blowfish and kingfish should hold steady as long as the water stays warm and clean. I'd treat weakfish and stripers as bonus fish this week, not the main event, and plan your trip around the tide, not the calendar.
